\chapter{Naming Who Someone Is}
\label{ch:te-roles}
\hlchaptermodality{48}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what someone's role is in Telugu --- teacher, student, doctor, farmer, guest --- and name the root that two of those words share.}

Complete TE-C48-guest and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[guruvu]{\te{గురువు} (guruvu) — a teacher}

\label{lesson:TE-C48-teacher}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{kaḍupu} mean, and what did \emph{vēlu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గురువు}}
\textbf{\te{గురువు}} (\emph{guruvu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a teacher\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{guru} means \textquotedblleft{}heavy\textquotedblright{}. The teacher is the weighty one — the one whose word carries weight — and Telugu added its own \textbf{-\te{వు}} to make \te{గురువు}.

You have already said the word without being told. \te{గురువారం}, Thursday, is Guru's day: the guru there is Jupiter, the heaviest wanderer the naked eye can find and the teacher of the gods. Latin named the same weekday for Jove, which is the same planet under another name.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five roles.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{guruvu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{guruvu}, then \emph{guruvāraṁ}, and say what the two have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గురువు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a teacher\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vidyārthi]{\te{విద్యార్థి} (vidyārthi) — a student}

\label{lesson:TE-C48-student}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{guruvu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{విద్యార్థి}}
\textbf{\te{విద్యార్థి}} (\emph{vidyārthi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a student\textquotedblright{}.

Two Sanskrit pieces welded: \emph{vidyā}, knowledge, and \emph{arthin}, one who seeks. A student is a knowledge-seeker, and the word says so on its face.

\emph{vidyā} grows from the root \emph{vid}, \textquotedblleft{}to know\textquotedblright{} — the same ancient root behind English \emph{wit} and \emph{wisdom}, and behind Latin \emph{vidēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}. Knowing and seeing were one word long before either language existed.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: a teacher and a student.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vidyārthi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{guruvu}, then \emph{vidyārthi}, and say which one seeks and which one weighs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{విద్యార్థి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a student\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vaidyuḍu]{\te{వైద్యుడు} (vaidyuḍu) — a doctor, a physician}

\label{lesson:TE-C48-doctor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vidyārthi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{వైద్యుడు}}
\textbf{\te{వైద్యుడు}} (\emph{vaidyuḍu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a doctor, a physician\textquotedblright{}.

Look at the middle of it. \emph{vaidya} is built on the very \emph{vid} sitting inside \te{విద్యార్థి}: a physician is one versed in the knowledge, the knowledge in question being \dv{आयुर्वेद}, the science of long life.

The ending \textbf{-\te{ుడు}} is not Sanskrit's but Telugu's own, marking a masculine person — the same \textbf{-\te{ుడు}} already carried by \te{స్నేహితుడు}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three roles, and two of them share a root.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vaidyuḍu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vidyārthi}, then \emph{vaidyuḍu}, and name the syllable they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{వైద్యుడు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a doctor, a physician\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[raitu]{\te{రైతు} (raitu) — a farmer}

\label{lesson:TE-C48-farmer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vaidyuḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{రైతు}}
\textbf{\te{రైతు}} (\emph{raitu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a farmer\textquotedblright{}.

\te{రైతు} came the long way round. Arabic \emph{raʿiyyah} meant a flock, then the people a ruler answers for. Persian and Urdu carried it into India as \emph{raʿīyat}, the subject, the tenant; the revenue clerks of the Deccan wrote it on their rolls; and Telugu kept it for the person who works the land.

That is a second arrival from the north-west, after \te{రోజు} and \te{పుస్తకం}. The words that travel are the words that follow paperwork and trade.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{raitu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{raitu}, then \emph{rōju}, and say what road the two have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{రైతు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a farmer\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[atithi]{\te{అతిథి} (atithi) — a guest}

\label{lesson:TE-C48-guest}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{raitu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{అతిథి}}
\textbf{\te{అతిథి}} (\emph{atithi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a guest\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{a-tithi} — \textquotedblleft{}one without a \emph{tithi}\textquotedblright{}, without a date on the calendar. The guest is defined by not being expected.

The old formula \te{అతిథి} \te{దేవో} \te{భవ}, \textquotedblleft{}let the guest be a god to you\textquotedblright{}, is built on exactly that: you cannot prepare for a god who arrives unannounced, so you keep the house ready instead. What a Telugu house actually does when the \te{అతిథి} arrives has a chapter of its own, at the end of this book.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five roles: a teacher, a student, a doctor, a farmer, a guest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{atithi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five, then say \emph{nā pēru} and your own name, and ask \emph{mīru evaru?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{అతిథి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a guest\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
